content: Helium (He) is a colorless, odorless, tasteless, non-toxic, and chemically inert monatomic element. It is the lightest member of the noble gases and has an atomic number of 2. Among all elements, helium has the lowest boiling and melting points, existing only as a gas under standard conditions, except in extreme environments. Helium compounds are rare and unstable at standard temperature and pressure, requiring extreme conditions for their formation. Helium has two stable isotopes: helium-4, which is the most common, and helium-3, which is rare. The behavior of liquid helium-4, particularly its two fluid phases (helium I and helium II), is of significant interest in quantum mechanics research, especially in studying superfluidity and the effects of near-absolute zero temperatures, such as superconductivity. Helium is the second most abundant element in the universe, following hydrogen, and is believed to have been created during the Big Bang. In the modern universe, new helium is primarily produced through the nuclear fusion of hydrogen in stars. On Earth, helium is generated by the radioactive decay of heavier elements, with alpha particles (helium nuclei) being trapped in natural gas deposits. These deposits can contain up to 7% helium by volume, and the gas is extracted through fractional distillation. Helium was first detected in 1868 by French astronomer Pierre Janssen, who observed an unknown yellow spectral line during a solar eclipse. This discovery was later confirmed by English astronomer Norman Lockyer, who named the element after the Greek word for the Sun, helios. Helium was first isolated on Earth in 1895 by British chemist William Ramsay, who identified it in the mineral cleveite. Helium is widely used in various applications due to its unique properties. It is employed in cryogenics, particularly for cooling superconducting magnets in MRI machines, and in deep-sea breathing systems to reduce risks such as nitrogen narcosis and decompression sickness. Helium is also used as a lifting gas for balloons and airships, as a shielding gas in arc welding, and as a protective atmosphere for growing silicon wafers and preserving historical documents. Additionally, helium is critical in space exploration, where it is used to pressurize and purge fuel systems and to cool liquid hydrogen and oxygen for rocket fuel. In its gaseous state, helium has high thermal conductivity, specific heat, and sound conduction velocity, surpassed only by hydrogen. Its low molecular mass and small atomic size allow it to diffuse through solids at a rate three times that of air. Helium is also the least water-soluble gas and has an index of refraction closest to unity among all gases. At normal ambient temperatures, helium exhibits a negative Joule-Thomson coefficient, meaning it heats up when allowed to expand freely. However, below its inversion temperature of approximately 40 K, helium cools upon expansion and can be liquefied. In its liquid state, helium exhibits remarkable quantum mechanical properties. Below its lambda point (approximately 2.17 K), helium-4 transitions into a superfluid state known as helium II. This state is characterized by zero viscosity, high thermal conductivity, and the ability to flow through tiny capillaries without resistance. Helium II also demonstrates unique behaviors such as the creeping effect, where it climbs the walls of a container, and the fountain effect, where it flows against gravity when heated. These phenomena are explained by the two-fluid model, which describes helium II as a mixture of superfluid and normal fluid components. Helium is extracted on a large scale from natural gas through fractional distillation. The process involves cooling and compressing the gas to liquefy other components, leaving behind crude helium, which is further purified to achieve a purity of 99.995%. Most helium is then liquefied for applications requiring liquid helium or for cost-effective transportation. Helium has two stable isotopes, helium-3 and helium-4. Helium-4 is the most abundant and is produced through the alpha decay of radioactive elements. Helium-3, while rare on Earth, is more abundant in stars and is a product of nuclear fusion. The isotopic composition of helium varies depending on its source, and this variability is used in geology to study the origin of rocks and the Earth's mantle composition. Helium-3 has potential applications in nuclear fusion, and its presence in lunar regolith has sparked interest in mining it for energy production. Exotic helium isotopes, such as helium-6 and helium-8, exhibit nuclear halos and are produced in specific nuclear reactions, but they decay rapidly into other substances.
